title: In Defence of the Long Novel
standfirst: Why the books that ask the most of us still give the most back.
body: There is a common complaint that nobody has time for long books any more. Our attention, we are told, has been broken into pieces by phones and feeds. Perhaps. Yet the long novel keeps finding readers, and there are good reasons why.

A long novel does something a short one cannot. It lets you live alongside its people. You see them make mistakes, change their minds and grow old. By the end you know them the way you know a friend of many years, with all their faults on show.

That effect cannot be hurried. It comes from the hours you spend in the book, and from the small, ordinary scenes that a shorter work would cut. The dinners, the walks and the letters are where the people become real.

Many of the great nineteenth-century novels came out in monthly parts. Readers waited weeks for the next instalment and talked about the characters in between. The length was not a burden. It was the pleasure itself, stretched out over a year or more.

Start with a book you have always meant to read, and give it twenty minutes a day. Do not race. Let a chapter sit before you start the next. Within a fortnight the habit forms, and the book becomes a place you look forward to returning to.
Long novels ask a lot of us. They ask for patience, attention and time. In return they offer something rarer than entertainment: the sense of having lived a second life alongside your own.
